concept.name: Back-running
concept.definition: Back-running is an MEV strategy in which a bot places its transaction immediately after a target transaction in the same block, profiting from the state change the target creates — most commonly arbitraging a price dislocation right after a large trade or an oracle update.
concept.intuition: Instead of jumping the queue, the bot waits for your transaction to move the market, then cleans up the mispricing you left behind in the very same block.
concept.mechanics: Searchers simulate the post-state of pending transactions (e.g. a large DEX swap that unbalances a pool, or a liquidation event) and submit a transaction that must execute directly after — buying the now-cheap asset on one venue and selling on another atomically. Placement is bought via gas bidding or bundle submission to block builders; the second leg of a sandwich attack is a back-run.
concept.failure_modes: Competition is so intense that most profit is bid away to validators as gas/bribes (searchers may pay >90% of MEV revenue in fees); failed back-runs still cost gas, and racing bots can make the trade revert.
concept.misconceptions: Back-running is not parasitic in all cases — DEX arbitrage back-runs are what keep AMM prices aligned with external markets, a service the ecosystem depends on; the harmful variant is when it extracts value from users (e.g. sandwiches).
concept.example: A 1,000 ETH sell on Uniswap pushes ETH's pool price 2% below Binance; a back-running bot buys ETH in the same block right after the sell and offloads it on a centralized exchange, pocketing the spread minus fees.

citations.source: Ethereum.org developer docs - Maximal extractable value (MEV)
Daian et al., Flash Boys 2.0: Frontrunning, Transaction Reordering, and Consensus Instability in Decentralized Exchanges
